overview.summary: Astronomers study planets, stars, galaxies and the universe, using telescopes, space missions and computer analysis to understand how it works.
overview.problems: They try to answer big questions about how the universe began, how stars and planets form and whether life might exist elsewhere.
overview.worksWith: Other scientists, engineers, telescope technicians, students and sometimes space agencies.
overview.workplaces: Universities, observatories, research institutes and space agencies, mostly in offices and computer rooms, with some time at telescopes.

timeline.title: Reading and planning
timeline.description: The astronomer reads new papers and plans observations or analysis.

timeline.title: Analyzing data
timeline.description: The astronomer processes images and measurements from telescopes using software.
timeline.why: Most astronomy is now done with computers.

timeline.title: Writing code and models
timeline.description: The astronomer builds simulations and tests ideas.
timeline.why: Models show whether an idea fits what is observed.

timeline.title: Meetings and teaching
timeline.description: The astronomer discusses results with colleagues and teaches or guides students.
timeline.why: Research is shared and checked by others.

timeline.title: Observing
timeline.description: The astronomer uses telescopes, often remotely, in clear weather.
timeline.why: Good observing time is rare and valuable.

timeline.title: Applying and writing
timeline.description: The astronomer applies for telescope time and funding and writes papers.
timeline.why: Access to telescopes and money is competitive.

responsibilities: Applying for telescope time and funding
Sharing results with other scientists and the public
challenges: Jobs are very competitive and often short-term, especially early in a career.
Telescope time depends on weather and competition.
Much of the work is computer analysis and writing.
Results may take years to appear.
workEnvironment: Offices, computer rooms and sometimes observatories, which can be on mountains or in remote places. Work is often independent, with regular collaboration and conferences. Hours can include nights for observing.
tradeoffs: Pay and opportunities that vary by country and institution

activity.title: Sketch the Moon for a week
steps: With an adult, find a safe spot where you can see the Moon in the evening sky.
Each clear evening for a week, draw its shape and note the date and time.
Compare your drawings and describe how it changes.
Read a trusted guide on why the Moon has phases.
Note whether patient observing felt interesting.
activity.outcome: You practise regular observation, recording and explaining a pattern.
activity.safety: Never look directly at the Sun, even with binoculars or a telescope, because it can cause permanent blindness. Observe at night only with an adult nearby and away from roads.

source: Written by Futurixia from general knowledge of how this profession works. It is illustrative and is not based on interviews or surveys.
